ideas.hypothesis: The ACA's 2014 ban on pre-existing-condition exclusions and rating lowered out-of-pocket spending and catastrophic health expenditure for nonelderly adults with chronic conditions such as cancer, relative to adults without such conditions. It also raised average nongroup premiums.

sources.role: mechanism and setting: from 2014 the ACA bars insurers from denying coverage or charging more for pre-existing conditions, which matters for cancer patients
setting: ACA design via Medicaid expansion and private insurance regulation
mechanism: reform expected to raise overall costs and pressure hospitals
comparison: Medicare's original aim of financial protection from catastrophic costs for people over 65

ideas.test: Run a triple-difference on MEPS, 2010-2017. Groups are adults aged 50-64 with or without a pre-existing chronic condition, before and after 2014, with adults aged 66-75 on Medicare as a second control. Outcomes are out-of-pocket spending above 10% of family income and individual-market premiums.
ideas.disconfirming: Out-of-pocket burden for 50-64-year-olds with pre-existing conditions does not fall relative to those without conditions, after differencing out the Medicare-age trend.

ideas.hypothesis: Across high-income democracies, greater political inequality, measured by the income gap in voter turnout, is associated with lower health system efficiency, meaning higher per capita health spending for a given life expectancy.

sources.role: mechanism: political inequality as a cause of the poor US health profile despite the highest spending
finding: the US ranks last among 17 peer countries in male life expectancy despite the highest spending
setting: policy proposals for a high-performance US health system
mechanism: market competition (HMOs) as an alternative policy route to system performance

ideas.test: Use an OECD panel of about 25 countries, 1990-2015, with per capita health spending, life expectancy and income-group turnout gaps from election studies. Estimate a stochastic frontier of life expectancy on spending and controls, with inefficiency modeled as a function of the turnout gap. Replicate across US states using CPS voting supplements.
ideas.disconfirming: The turnout gap is unrelated to health system inefficiency, or higher political inequality goes with more efficient systems.

ideas.hypothesis: In high-prevalence settings, regular surveillance of high-risk carriers for liver cancer leads to earlier-stage diagnosis, lower first-year treatment costs and lower lifetime cost per QALY than diagnosis without surveillance, enough to make surveillance cost-saving within ten years.

sources.role: method: lifetime survival extrapolation (semiparametric) with EQ-5D utilities and reimbursed costs from Taiwan national insurance
method and measure: population-based costing of the three months before and the first year after diagnosis for common cancers using linked registry and administrative data

ideas.test: Link Taiwan National Health Insurance claims to the cancer registry for hepatitis B and C carriers diagnosed with liver cancer, 2000-2015. Compare carriers with regular ultrasound and AFP surveillance in the two years before diagnosis with those without it on stage at diagnosis, costs from three months before to one year after diagnosis, and extrapolated lifetime survival and QALYs. Adjust with propensity scores.
ideas.disconfirming: Surveilled patients show no stage shift, no lower first-year costs, or a cost per QALY above conventional thresholds once surveillance costs are included.

ideas.hypothesis: State reforms that combine community rating or guaranteed issue with an individual mandate (the Massachusetts model) lower uninsurance without shrinking the individual market. Community rating without a mandate shrinks individual-market enrollment and raises premiums.

sources.role: method and data: state panel, 1987-2007, of party control and state policy reforms against uninsurance rates
setting: early results from the Massachusetts Chapter 58 reform with an individual mandate
measure: gaps in individual-market benefit coverage (mental health and substance use) that reform addressed
outcome context: hospital financial condition as reforms expanded coverage

ideas.test: Build a state panel, 1990-2013, coding guaranteed issue, community rating and mandate provisions. Outcomes are uninsurance (CPS/ACS) and individual-market enrollment and premiums (from insurer filings). Estimate a difference-in-differences with separate treatment indicators for rating reform alone and rating reform plus mandate, with state and year fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: Rating reforms without a mandate do not shrink individual-market enrollment, or the mandate combination does not lower uninsurance more than rating reform alone.

ideas.hypothesis: ACA coverage expansion cut uncompensated care most at hospitals that were financially weak before the reform. Private premium growth slowed in their markets because less cost was shifted to private payers.

sources.role: measure: pre-ACA (2011) financial condition analysis of US hospitals facing higher volumes at lower reimbursement
setting: national reform modeled on Massachusetts's near-universal, affordable coverage design
mechanism: employers' interest in reform follows whether private remedies are containing health cost inflation

ideas.test: Merge Medicare hospital cost reports, 2011-2017 (uncompensated care, operating margins), with employer-sponsored or marketplace premium data by market area. Run a difference-in-differences comparing Medicaid expansion and non-expansion states, with treatment intensity set by the hospital's 2011 financial-condition score. The outcomes are the change in uncompensated care and local private premium growth.
ideas.disconfirming: Financially weak hospitals in expansion states see no larger drop in uncompensated care, or local private premium growth does not slow relative to non-expansion markets.

ideas.hypothesis: The change from pre-ACA individual premiums to exchange benchmark premiums is larger in rating areas with more concentrated hospital markets and fewer participating insurers. Provider market power is passed through to individual-market prices.

sources.role: method and data: tax data on self-employed premiums compared with reference silver exchange premiums (4.2% higher before subsidies)
mechanism: the US health market moving toward concentration and oligopoly, with weak cost containment
setting: a state reform restructuring the individual market
mechanism: supply-side policy changes in delivery can raise rather than cut medical costs

ideas.test: Aggregate pre-2014 self-employed premium deductions per covered person by rating area (or use another pre-ACA individual premium source). Match them to 2014 benchmark silver premiums, hospital HHI and the number of exchange insurers. Regress the log premium change on HHI and insurer count, controlling for age mix and health status.
ideas.disconfirming: Premium changes are unrelated to hospital concentration and insurer count, or are smaller in concentrated markets.

ideas.hypothesis: Raising CHIP copayments for office visits and outpatient services shifts children's care toward emergency department visits and avoidable inpatient admissions. Total cost per enrollee does not fall even though outpatient use declines.

sources.role: method and data: segmented regression on Alabama ALL Kids claims around the 2004 copayment increase, covering inpatient, ED, drugs and office visits
measure: spending split into inpatient, hospital outpatient, office-based and pharmacy categories
finding: outpatient volumes respond strongly to changes in local supply and access

ideas.test: Use Alabama ALL Kids claims, 1999-2009, in an interrupted time series with a comparison group of enrollees exempt from copays (lowest income tier). Outcomes per 1,000 member-months are office visits, ED visits, ambulatory-care-sensitive hospitalizations and total allowed cost.
ideas.disconfirming: ED visits and avoidable admissions do not rise relative to the exempt group after the copay increase, and total cost per enrollee falls.

ideas.hypothesis: Legal uncertainty over the individual mandate during the 2010-2012 litigation slowed insurer entry and exchange preparation. States that were plaintiffs in anti-mandate suits had fewer insurers and higher benchmark premiums in the 2014 marketplaces, holding market fundamentals fixed.

sources.role: setting: state-actor litigation (Kinder v. Geithner) challenging the mandate's constitutionality
mechanism: split lower-court rulings on Commerce Clause authority created legal uncertainty
setting: the Supreme Court ruling that upheld the ACA and ended the main uncertainty
mechanism: state-insurer agreements shape how insurers participate in state markets

ideas.test: Build a state cross-section for 2014: participation in anti-mandate lawsuits, number of marketplace insurers, benchmark silver premium, exchange type, Medicaid expansion, pre-ACA individual-market concentration and population health. Regress insurer count and premium on plaintiff status with these controls, and check robustness using 2015-2016 to see whether gaps closed.
ideas.disconfirming: Plaintiff states have the same insurer counts and premiums as other states once exchange type, Medicaid expansion and market structure are controlled for.

ideas.hypothesis: SCHIP enrollment raises children's outpatient visit use more in areas served by integrated delivery systems that own ambulatory and home health businesses than in areas served mainly by standalone hospitals. Supply-side organization moderates how coverage turns into outpatient access.

sources.role: data and finding: surveys of 16,700 SCHIP enrollees in ten states, comparing new, established and disenrolled enrollees on access and service use
measure: scope of integrated delivery systems across ambulatory, acute, subacute and home health businesses (HIMSS data)
setting: the federally required package of outpatient, clinic and home health benefits in public child coverage
finding: local delivery-system supply changes reshape outpatient utilization

ideas.test: Merge the ten-state SCHIP enrollee survey with county-level measures of integrated-system ambulatory and home health ownership. Compare outpatient visits and unmet-need rates of established enrollees with new enrollees (the baseline group), interacted with local integrated-system scope, controlling for child health and demographics.
ideas.disconfirming: The enrollment-related gain in outpatient use is the same where integrated systems have broad ambulatory scope and where they do not.

ideas.hypothesis: Among insured adults, enrollment in high-deductible or consumer-directed plans raises reported cost-related access problems, especially in rural areas. Coverage gains through such plans therefore improve affordability less than coverage through low-deductible plans.

sources.role: mechanism: consumer-directed health plans as an insurer strategy for affordability and quality
setting and measure: rural residents' perceptions of health care access and affordability over a decade
measure: metropolitan trends in insured versus uninsured status

ideas.test: Use NHIS or MEPS, 2007-2017, to identify adults by plan type (HDHP or consumer-directed versus traditional) and rural or urban residence. Regress delayed or forgone care due to cost on plan type, rurality and their interaction, controlling for income, health status and employer characteristics.
ideas.disconfirming: HDHP enrollees report no more cost-related access problems than traditional plan enrollees, or the gap is not larger in rural areas.
